items.title: Delayed Adjuvant Systemic Therapy Versus Standard of Care (Observation Without Adjuvant Therapy) in Patients Ineligible for Timely Adjuvant Therapy After Resection of Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
In this randomized clinical trial, the investigators will study whether the participants with pancreatic cancer can benefit from starting chemotherapy later than usual after surgery. The investigators will compare two groups of patients:

Patients who start adjuvant chemotherapy between 13 and 24 weeks after surgery. Patients who receive no adjuvant chemotherapy, which is the current standard approach if treatment could not be started within 12 weeks after surgery.

Patients who have recovered sufficiently from surgery between 13 and 24 weeks after their operation, and who show no signs of cancer recurrence or spread, can participate in the study. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two groups. Patients receiving treatment will be given one of the standard chemotherapy regimens routinely used in clinical practice.

All patients will be followed with CT scans and blood tests for tumor markers every six months for five years.

For patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the overall survival after surgery is strongly linked to whether they receive adjuvant chemotherapy. Pancreatic surgery is a major operation with a high risk of complications. As a result, many patients do not recover well enough to start chemotherapy within the 12 weeks recommended by international guidelines. These patients are therefore often left without any additional treatment after surgery.

It is currently unclear whether starting adjuvant chemotherapy later than 12 weeks after surgery is still beneficial. Some retrospective studies suggest that delayed treatment may improve survival compared with surgery alone. However, these studies have included relatively few patients and were not designed to provide definitive answers.

The patients targeted in this study represent an important group that has largely been overlooked in previous clinical trials. The question of whether delayed adjuvant chemotherapy can improve outcomes is recognized internationally as a major unanswered research question. Because patients treated with surgery alone generally have poorer survival, it is important to determine whether delayed chemotherapy can still provide meaningful benefit.

interventions: Delayed adjuvant standard systemic chemotherapy given within 13-24 weeks after pancreatic cancer surgery, outside the standardized interval within 12 weeks after surgery

items.title: Targeting the "Undruggable": Advances in RAS Inhibition for Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Over 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC) harbor oncogenic KRAS mutations, a target long considered therapeutically undruggable. Advances in structure-based drug design have now yielded allele-selective and multiselective inhibitors capable of directly targeting mutant RAS. Recently, in the phase 3 RASolute-302 trial, the multiselective RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib significantly improved overall survival over standard chemotherapy in patients with previously treated metastatic PDAC, marking the first positive randomized trial of a RAS-directed agent in this disease. However, major questions and challenges remain, including acquired resistance, toxicity, and optimal sequencing. In this review, we examine the KRAS-mutant landscape of PDAC, emerging classes of RAS inhibitors, clinical evidence, resistance mechanisms, and rational combination strategies that are shaping this rapidly evolving field.

items.title: Multimodal Biomarkers in Pancreatic Cancer: From Early Detection to Precision Therapy.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains highly lethal, with a 5-year relative survival of ∼13%. For decades, CA19-9 has been the principal clinical biomarker, but its limitations-including nonsecretion in Lewis-negative individuals, false-positive elevations with cholestasis, and inadequate sensitivity for early detection-have driven a rapidly expanding biomarker landscape. Blood-based multianalyte assays integrating circulating proteins, glycoproteins, methylated cell-free DNA, and tumor-derived signals, together with imaging-based deep learning, are improving early detection beyond CA19-9 alone. Molecular subtyping and postoperative circulating tumor DNA further refine prognosis, while germline and somatic alterations-including BRCA1/2/PALB2, MSI-H/dMMR, NRG1 fusions, KRAS G12C, NTRK, FGFR2, and BRAF V600E-are increasingly enabling biomarker-directed therapy. The next frontier is prospective validation and clinical integration of multimodal biomarkers to enable earlier diagnosis, more precise risk stratification, and equitable delivery of precision therapy.

items.title: Targeting KCa3.1 channels in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma impairs disease progression.
items.abstract: This study explores the therapeutic potential of the calcium-activated potassium channel KCa3.1 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Increased KCa3.1 expression correlates with poor overall survival of patients with PDAC. Using the immunocompetent KPfC (KrasWT/LSL-G12D Tp53fl/+ Pdx1-Cre) mouse model, we evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of KCa3.1 inhibition with TRAM-34 and maurotoxin alone or in combination with gemcitabine. Mechanistic insights were obtained in vitro from KCa3.1 CRISPR knockout pancreatic cancer cells (PANC-1KCNN4-/-) and a three-dimensional mixed spheroid model composed of pancreatic cancer and stellate cells. In vivo, KCa3.1 inhibition combined with gemcitabine decreased growth of tumor nodes and counteracted gemcitabine-induced fibrosis. Consistently, in vitro and ex vivo data showed that KCa3.1 inhibition induced tumor cell death and altered the invasive phenotype. Here, maurotoxin outperformed TRAM-34. On a molecular level, KCa3.1 inhibition diminished epithelial-mesenchymal transition, reduced T cell exhaustion markers and TGF-β1 secretion, and downregulated the G2-M checkpoint. These findings can mechanistically account for the therapeutic benefits of targeting KCa3.1 channels in PDAC.

items.title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Circulating Tumor DNA Provide Distinct Prognostic Signals in Localized Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the third leading cause of cancer death in the US. Socioeconomic disadvantage, measured by Area Deprivation Index (ADI), may affect outcomes beyond tumor biology. We evaluate ADI and overall survival (OS) in localized PDAC, accounting for KRAS-mutant circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).
METHODS: 165 patients with localized PDAC were prospectively enrolled (NCT04616131; Oct. 2020-Jan. 2026). ADI was dichotomized at the 50th national percentile. OS was compared by group and jointly with ctDNA using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Multivariable Cox assessed ADI and survival, adjusting for clinical covariates and ctDNA, and tested ADI/ctDNA interactions. C-index/likelihood ratio assessed added discriminatory value. Next-generation sequencing detected KRAS-mutant ctDNA.
RESULTS: High ADI was associated with shorter OS (26.7 vs 30.5 months, p=0.035; HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.09-2.92, p=0.020). Patients with both high ADI and detectable ctDNA had the poorest survival (9.8 vs 38.3 months, p=0.005). ADI and ctDNA each independently predicted shorter survival without significant interaction; combining both improved model discrimination beyond either alone.
CONCLUSION: Greater area deprivation is associated with reduced survival in localized PDAC, independently of clinical and tumor biomarkers. ADI and ctDNA may have additive value for risk stratification, supporting interventions targeting social determinants alongside oncologic care.

items.title: A Phase I/II Single-Arm, Open-Label, Exploratory Study Evaluating the Safety and Efficacy of Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT) Combined With Gemcitabine and Iparomlimab-Toripalimab in Borderline Resectable Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: This is a Phase I/II, single-arm, open-label, exploratory study aimed at evaluating the safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) combined with gemcitabine and iparomlimab-toripalimab in patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer. The study is divided into two phases: The Phase Ib dose-escalation phase will use a "3+3" design to explore the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of SBRT (6 Gy×5 F, 7 Gy×5 F, 8 Gy×5 F) combined with gemcitabine and iparomlimab-toripalimab. The Phase II phase will further evaluate the efficacy and safety of this combination regimen based on the SBRT dose determined in Phase Ib. The primary efficacy endpoint is the R0 resection rate.

items.title: Patient-Derived Organoids in Pancreatic Cancer Pharmacology: From Pharmacotyping Methodology to the AVATAR Phase III Trial and the Pharmacological Frontier.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) carries a five-year survival below 13%, and most patients receive empirical first-line chemotherapy that has advanced only modestly in two decades. Pharmacological progress has been constrained by two features of the disease: a mutational landscape dominated by KRAS mutations until recently considered undruggable, and a desmoplastic stroma that obstructs both cytotoxic and immunological intervention. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs), three-dimensional cultures grown from primary or biopsy tumour tissue, have become the dominant functional platform in PDAC pharmacology, supporting drug-sensitivity profiling, combination screening, and drug-delivery evaluation in patient-matched culture. The 2025 AVATAR Phase III trial provided the first randomised evaluation of an integrated genomic, PDO, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) personalised pharmacotherapy strategy in metastatic PDAC. It reported no intention-to-treat survival benefit (median overall survival 8.6 versus 8.7 months, p = 0.849). Of the 39 experimental-arm patients who proceeded to a second or subsequent line, 35 did not receive matched therapy, and clinical deterioration was the leading reason, recorded in 26. Yet the four patients (10%) who did receive matched therapy reached a median overall survival of 19.3 months. Because this subgroup was very small (n = 4) and non-randomised, that observation is exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, and it points to operational constraints as the dominant limit on clinical performance. This review synthesises the AVATAR result with the foundational pharmacotyping framework of Tiriac et al (2018), the chemoresistance and combination-pharmacology literature, and recent KRAS-inhibitor screens, clarifying what PDOs can and cannot accomplish for patients with PDAC in 2026. Pharmacological priorities for the field are addressed in detail, principally compressing the diagnostic pipeline and integrating stromal co-culture so that combination-library design rests on biologically faithful drug-response prediction.

items.title: Prospective Evidence of Concomitant Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Risk Among Patients With Branch-duct Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms Without Worrisome Features/High-risk Stigmata at Baseline.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the natural history, especially concomitant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (cPDAC) risk in patients with branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (BD-IPMN) without worrisome features (WF) or high-risk stigmata (HRS).
SUMMARY BACKGROUND DATA: BD-IPMNs without WF/HRS are considered low-risk, yet optimal surveillance strategies remain uncertain.
METHODS: In a prospective multicenter Japan Pancreas Society registry, 1234 patients with BD-IPMN without WF/HRS underwent imaging and laboratory surveillance every 6 months for up to 5.17 years. Cumulative incidence, standardized incidence ratios (SIRs), and competing-risk analyses were performed to assess advanced pancreatic neoplasia, defined as IPMN high-grade dysplasia (IPMN-HGD), invasive IPMN, or cPDAC, and associated risk factors. Outcomes were also evaluated under simulated guideline-recommended extended surveillance intervals.
RESULTS: During 5.17 years of follow-up, advanced pancreatic neoplasia developed in 26 patients: 10 IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN and 16 cPDAC. The 5.17-year cumulative incidence was 2.48%; SIRs relative to the general population were 8.01 overall, 3.07 for IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN, and 4.91 for cPDAC. The cPDAC SIRs were 6.21 and 3.02 for cysts <20 mm and ≥20 mm, respectively. Diabetes history and mural nodule development predicted IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN, whereas CA19-9 elevation and new or worsening diabetes predicted cPDAC. Of 19 patients eligible for surveillance interval extension, 13 (68%) had a later simulated detection date.
CONCLUSION: Patients with BD-IPMN without WF/HRS at baseline had 3.07 and 4.91 times the incidences of IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN and cPDAC expected in the general population, respectively. Surveillance based solely on cyst stability may warrant caution regarding the timely detection of surgically resectable pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Iparomlimab and Tuvonralimab Injection （QL1706）Combined With Chemotherapy (AG) and SBRT as First-Line Treatment for Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if the study drug QL1706 (iparomlimab and tuvonralimab injection) works to treat locally advanced pancreatic cancer in adults when it is given together with chemotherapy and Stereotactic radiotherapy. It will also learn about the safety of this combination treatment.

Around 37 adults aged 18 to 75 who have pancreatic cancer that has grown into nearby tissue and cannot be removed by surgery, but has not spread to other parts of the body, and who have not yet received any treatment for it, will take part in this study.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does the combination of QL1706, chemotherapy and radiation make the tumor shrink or stop growing, making it suitable for surgery? How long do participants live without their cancer getting worse, and how long do they live overall? What medical problems do participants have when taking this combination treatment? All participants in this study will receive the same treatment. There is no placebo (a look-alike substance that contains no drug) and no comparison group. Researchers will compare the results of participants in this study with the results usually seen in people who receive chemotherapy alone, to see if adding QL1706 and radiation helps.

Participants will:

Receive QL1706 through a vein (by intravenous infusion) once every 3 weeks Receive 2 chemotherapy drugs through a vein on days 1 and 8 of every 3-week cycle, for 2 cycles. The 2 drugs are gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel Then receive 5 doses of focused radiation therapy to the pancreas, given about every other day over about 2 weeks, together with 2 more cycles of QL1706 and chemotherapy. Participants whose cancer gets worse during treatment will stop this part of the study Have CT or MRI scans every 6 weeks so the researchers can see whether the cancer has shrunk Have blood tests, physical examinations and other checkups during treatment Be reviewed by a team of pancreatic cancer specialists to see if surgery to remove the tumor is possible. Participants who can have surgery will have the surgery and then 2 to 4 more cycles of QL1706 and chemotherapy. Participants who cannot have surgery, and whose cancer has not grown, will keep receiving QL1706 and chemotherapy until their cancer gets worse, the treatment becomes too hard to tolerate, or they are no longer able to take part Tell the study team about any medical problems they have, which will be recorded throughout the study.

items.title: Identification of Biomarkers Using Quantitative Imaging for Phenotyping and Predicting Treatment Response in Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a major health problem, characterized by a rising incidence and limited treatment options. There is an urgent need for in vivo imaging methods capable of reliably determining tumor subtype and of evaluating, from a prognostic standpoint, the response to neoadjuvant therapy in order to guide surgical resection.

The structural and mechanical properties of PDACs vary by tumor type and are likely to influence treatment response. Among MRI imaging techniques, diffusion-weighted MRI is sensitive to the structural properties of tissues, while elastography is sensitive to their mechanical properties.

The MISTRA project aims to evaluate the performance of diffusion-weighted MRI and MRI elastography in determining tumor subtypes and predicting response to treatment.

items.title: [Position paper: surveillance for pancreatic cancer in individuals at elevated risk for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma].
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, where treatment options are limited. Studies suggest that early detection programs for individuals with increased genetic or familial risk may enable diagnosis and surgical treatment at a potentially curable stage. Early detection programs for pancreatic cancer show effectiveness and are cost-effective in populations stratified by the appropriate age to initiate surveillance. There is no benefit in participating in such a program for individuals who are not interested in surgery or are not surgical candidates due to their medical condition. Annual surveillance with MRI or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is recommended for carriers of specific gene mutations-such as BRCA2, even without a family history of pancreatic cancer and for carriers of other genes only when a family history is present, or for individuals with a strong family history even without an identified genetic mutation. This position paper details surveillance recommendations for high-risk populations.

items.title: Hepatic Arterial Infusion Floxuridine with Systemic Therapy for Liver-dominant Metastatic Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: Results of the PANCPUMP Phase II Pilot Study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatic progression is common in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We evaluated hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) floxuridine (FUDR) added to systemic chemotherapy in selected patients with synchronous liver-dominant metastatic PDAC.
METHODS: PANCPUMP was a prospective, single-center, single-arm phase II pilot study of 14 patients with synchronous PDAC liver metastases and stable disease or response after at least 2 months of systemic chemotherapy. Patients underwent HAI pump placement and received up to six 28 day cycles of HAI FUDR with systemic therapy. The primary endpoint was 1 year hepatic progression-free survival, with a prespecified target of 40%.
RESULTS: Seven patients (50%) remained free of hepatic progression at 1 year, meeting the primary endpoint. Median time to hepatic progression was 15.7 months when deaths without hepatic progression were censored; median all-site progression-free interval and overall survival were 14.5 and 14.0 months, respectively. Five patients (35.7%) survived at least 24 months. Biochemical hepatotoxicity was frequent; two delayed grade 3 gastroduodenal artery (GDA)/catheter-associated vascular complications occurred. Among 10 patients with paired European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality-of-Life questionnaire assessments, the mean global health/quality-of-life score was 69.2 at baseline and 70.0 at first follow-up (p = 0.91).
CONCLUSIONS: HAI FUDR plus systemic therapy met the prespecified hepatic-control endpoint in a highly selected cohort. These proof-of-concept findings support further study of regional hepatic therapy alongside contemporary systemic treatment.

items.title: Deubiquitinating enzymes in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: signaling networks, biomarkers, and mechanism-guided combination strategies.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ubiquitination is a reversible post-translational modification dynamically regulated by ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs). By removing or editing ubiquitin chains on substrate proteins, deubiquitinating enzymes regulate protein stability, subcellular localization, signaling-complex assembly, and cellular stress responses. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by marked invasiveness, extensive metabolic reprogramming, pronounced therapeutic resistance, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment, highlighting the need for molecularly informed biomarkers and mechanism-guided therapeutic strategies. However, the translational interpretation of DUBs in PDAC remains challenging because DUBs often display broad substrate spectra, context-dependent functions, conserved catalytic domains, and uneven levels of experimental and clinical evidence.
MAIN BODY: Increasing evidence indicates that multiple DUBs regulate PDAC progression and therapeutic resistance through KRAS-RAS/MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo-YAP/TAZ, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Notch, NF-κB, autophagy, metabolism, immune evasion, and metastasis-related programs. In this review, we organize the available evidence according to DUB-substrate axes, ubiquitin linkage types, pathway dependency, model-system support, biomarker feasibility, and therapeutic readiness. We distinguish evidence derived from cell-based assays, animal models, organoids, patient-derived xenografts, patient tissues, public datasets, and clinical cohorts, and classify DUB-centered biomarkers according to their diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, or pharmacodynamic potential. We further summarize DUB-targeting strategies and mechanism-guided combinations with chemotherapy, metabolic intervention, DNA-damage response targeting, and immune checkpoint blockade, while emphasizing inhibitor selectivity, pharmacokinetic and toxicity limitations, resistance mechanisms, and clinical readiness.
CONCLUSION: DUB-centered translation in PDAC should be developed as an axis-based and evidence-ranked framework rather than as a single-target catalogue. The most promising near-term opportunities are likely to arise from DUB-substrate axes with defined mechanisms, measurable biomarker readouts, patient-derived or clinically annotated validation, pharmacodynamic indicators, and rational combination partners. Most DUB-targeted strategies in PDAC remain preclinical and require further validation before clinical implementation.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

items.title: MRI radiomics of pancreatic tumours: a systematic review of methodological quality and imaging reproducibility.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Radiomics holds potential for personalised treatment, but reproducibility is hindered by inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters and methodological details. This study aims to identify and evaluate key MR imaging parameters to support radiomics reproducibility and to systematically evaluate the quality of published MRI radiomics studies focused on pancreatic tumours.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The literature search was conducted in the Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases. Human studies investigating MRI radiomics in pancreatic tumours were included. An imaging reporting checklist was developed and used to identify and evaluate imaging parameters in eligible studies. The methodological quality score (METRICS) and checklist for evaluation of radiomics research (CLEAR) score were calculated for each study.
RESULTS: Seventy-eight studies, encompassing 241 MRI pulse sequences (143 anatomical and 98 functional), were included. The imaging checklist identified ten core items as key parameters for ensuring reproducible MRI radiomics. Across all studies, none provided complete or consistent reporting of these parameters, with frequent omissions in imaging acquisition and reconstruction details. Methodological and reporting quality remained suboptimal, reflected by median METRICS and CLEAR scores of 52.4% (45-60%) and 62.3% (56-69%), respectively. Reproducibility and quality of radiomics studies would benefit from clear reporting of imaging parameters, consistent documentation of radiomics settings, and control of confounding variables. Additionally, transparency in model validation, preprocessing, and explanation methods would further enhance reproducibility and clinical relevance.
CONCLUSION: A focused imaging reproducibility checklist has been developed, and it has been demonstrated that no pancreatic tumour MRI radiomics study reported all necessary imaging parameters for reproducibility. Methodological and reporting quality on broader radiomics components was also poor, highlighting the potential value of such a checklist for improving standardised reporting in radiomics studies.
KEY POINTS: Question There is inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters across MRI protocols used for pancreatic tumours radiomics analysis. Findings The developed MR imaging reporting checklist provides structured guidelines to promote consistent documentation of MR imaging parameters and support reproducible radiomics research. Relevance statement By identifying how key MR imaging acquisition and reconstruction parameters are currently presented in MRI radiomics studies of pancreatic tumours, this study highlights inconsistencies and omissions in reporting, underscoring the need for more transparent reporting and adherence to guidelines to support radiomics reproducibility.

items.title: Quantitative KRAS ctDNA Dynamics Predict Early Recurrence After Neoadjuvant Therapy and Surgery in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Early recurrence remains prevalent in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) despite multimodality treatment. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is an emerging prognostic biomarker showing promise in detecting minimal residual disease (MRD). Using a high-sensitivity digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) assay, we evaluated KRAS- mutant ctDNA as a marker of MRD associated with early recurrence (< 12 months) in patients with localized PDAC receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), surgery, and adjuvant chemotherapy (AC). KRAS G12D, G12V, and G12R mutations found in cell-free DNA were detected and quantified with maximum variant allele frequency (mVAF). Of 130 enrolled patients, 55 completed NAC and resection. ctDNA was detected a median of 7.6 months before imaging-confirmed recurrence. Postoperative detection KRAS ctDNA was independently associated with worse recurrence-free survival (RFS) (aHR 3.30, 95% CI 1.33-8.21, p = 0.010), and ctDNA clearance after NAC and surgery was independently associated with improved RFS (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.06-0.90, p = 0.035). Median cohort mVAF was 0.03%; patients with mVAF above the median had shorter RFS (12.8 vs. 26.3 months) and more frequent early recurrence (p = 0.027). ctDNA-positive patients who received AC remained with worse outcomes than ctDNA-negative patients, suggesting persistent chemotherapy resistance. These data indicated that persistent KRAS ctDNA after NAC and surgery reflects MRD and support sensitive postoperative ctDNA testing to stratify high risk patients for early recurrence, guiding quantitative, longitudinal monitoring. Future studies in adaptive treatment settings may further extend these findings toward ctDNA-guided clinical decision-making.

items.title: Fluid-derived pancreatic cancer organoids reveal CEMIP, CALB2, and LY6D as drivers of chemotherapy resistance.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies with few effective treatments and an urgent need for personalized therapeutic strategies. Although patient-derived organoids (PDOs) facilitate drug screening, tissue-derived models often require invasive sampling and suffer from low cellularity and contamination by non-tumor cells. In this study, we developed fluid-derived organoids (FDOs) from malignant effusions as a rapid, minimally invasive, and scalable platform for PDAC research.
METHODS: Organoids were isolated from the pleural effusion and ascitic fluid of patients with PDAC. Histopathological and molecular characterization, including KRAS mutation analysis and CK7 immunostaining, confirmed the tumor origin and biological fidelity. Holotomography was used to characterize organoid morphology and drug response. Drug sensitivity was evaluated using the KRAS G12D inhibitor, MRTX1133. Transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify resistance-associated molecular signatures, and functional validation was used to assess the roles of candidate genes.
RESULTS: FDOs were established with a higher success rate, faster growth, and lower non-tumor contamination than conventional tissue-derived PDOs, while faithfully recapitulating the parental tumor histology and genetics. KRAS G12D-mutant FDOs showed marked sensitivity to MRTX1133. Transcriptomic analysis revealed the upregulation of CEMIP, CALB2, and LY6D in chemo-resistant FDOs, with these genes suppressing apoptosis and conferring gemcitabine resistance in PDAC cells. High expression of this three-gene signature correlated with worse clinical outcomes, underscoring its prognostic and therapeutic relevance.
CONCLUSIONS: FDOs are an efficient and clinically relevant model for drug sensitivity profiling and biomarker discovery in patients with PDAC. The elevated expression of CEMIP, CALB2, and LY6D drives chemoresistance and poor prognosis, highlighting their value as predictive biomarkers and potential targets for overcoming pancreatic cancer resistance.

items.title: Conditional survival in pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma and ductal adenocarcinoma by SEER summary stage.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Survival measured from diagnosis does not directly describe future survival after pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (pACC) patients reach a survival landmark. We estimated conditional overall survival (OS) for pACC and assessed comparisons with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
METHODS: SEER 17 records included registry-coded pACC (8550/3) and PDAC (8140/3 or 8500/3) with histologic confirmation diagnosed during 2004-2023. Three- and five-year conditional OS estimates overall and by SEER Summary Stage included risk sets and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sensitivity analyses restricted diagnosis years to allow the prediction interval and used 8500-only PDAC.
RESULTS: The cohort contained 580 pACC and 115,936 PDAC tumors. Overall three-year conditional OS for pACC was 34.2% at diagnosis and 73.0% (95% CI, 60.5-82.2%) at the five-year landmark, with 76 records still observed. At that landmark, the 2004-2015 diagnosis cohort had three-year OS of 75.5% (61.5-84.9%; n = 53), whereas the 2004-2013 cohort had five-year OS of 74.4% (57.6-85.3%; n = 39). Estimates were higher at later landmarks within both common diagnosis cohorts. With 8500-only PDAC, the three-year OS difference was 9.2 percentage points at diagnosis and 7.7 at five years in the full cohort, versus 10.5 and 11.5 in the common 2004-2015 cohort.
CONCLUSIONS: Conditional OS provides population-level survival estimates for pACC landmark survivors. Comparisons with PDAC depend on its coding definition and the diagnosis cohort.

items.title: 177Lu-ACT319 in FAP Expressing Solid Tumors
items.abstract:
This is a study of 177Lu -ACT319 in participants with the following cancers: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), biliary tract carcinoma (BTC), that is advanced, and for which there are no valid treatment options. Participants must have cancer that expresses protein called fibroblast activation protein (FAP). The purpose of this study is to evaluate safety, how the body tolerates, and how well ACT319 works in treating cancer. In addition, this study will evaluate how much 177Lu-ACT319 gets into the bloodstream, how it is broken down, and how long it takes the body to get rid of it. For each participant, the study will last approximately 2 years.

A separate group of patients with other FAP expressing solid tumor types will be evaluated by PET/CT or SPECT/CT imaging for the intensity of target expression.

items.title: AKR1B1-dependent ferroptosis defense contributes to KRASG12C inhibitor resistance in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
AIMS: To investigate the role of AKR1B1-associated ferroptosis defense in acquired KRASG12Cinhibitor (G12Ci) resistance in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells, and to evaluate the antitumor activity of AKR1B1 inhibition combined with KRASG12C inhibition in xenograft models.
METHODS: Sotorasib- and adagrasib-resistant PDAC cell populations were analyzed using integrated genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic profiling. The functional roles of AKR1B1 and YAP1 were assessed using siRNA-mediated knockdown, ferroptosis-rescue assays, and pharmacological inhibition with epalrestat. The combination of epalrestat and sotorasib was also evaluated in treatment-naïve cell line-derived and patient-derived xenograft models.
RESULTS: Multi-omics profiling identified AKR1B1 upregulation in sotorasib- and adagrasib-resistant MIA PaCa-2 cells. In these in vitro resistant cell models, AKR1B1 knockdown reduced YAP1 and SLC7A11 expression and cystine uptake, while increasing lipid peroxidation. Epalrestat enhanced the growth-inhibitory effects of G12Ci in resistant cells, with localized synergy at selected concentrations. In treatment-naive MIA PaCa-2 CDX, KRASG12C-mutant PDX, and UMUC3 CDX models, epalrestat plus sotorasib suppressed tumor growth more than either agent alone.
CONCLUSIONS: AKR1B1-associated ferroptosis defense contributes to acquired KRAS G12Ci resistance in PDAC cell models, and AKR1B1 inhibition enhances sotorasib activity in treatment-naive xenograft models. These findings support further evaluation of AKR1B1 inhibition as a combination strategy for KRASG12Cmutant PDAC.

items.title: Enhanced prognosis stratification following surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to optimize clinical decisions by reflecting tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an extremely dismal postoperative prognosis. Conventional TNM staging cannot adequately characterize tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment, leading to suboptimal risk stratification. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an integrated prognostic system for PDAC by combining deep learning (DL)-based radiomic features with guideline‑recommended clinicopathological variables.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included 592 patients with PDAC who underwent R0 surgical resection. A Swin Transformer-assisted DL classifier (Outcome Prediction for PDAC, OP-PDAC) was built using multi-planar contrast-enhanced CT scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal planes). Radiogenomic analysis was conducted in 41 patients to elucidate the biological underpinnings of the OP-PDAC. Furthermore, the Intelligent Prognosis Stratification System (IPSS-PDAC) was developed by incorporating clinicopathological variables into the OP-PDAC framework.
RESULTS: In the derivation and test cohorts, the C‑index of OP-PDAC for predicting 1‑year disease‑free survival (DFS) ranged from 0.807 to 0.844, which was significantly higher than that of the clinicopathological model (CP-PDAC; C‑index, 0.631-0.656). The IPSS-PDAC further enhanced predictive performance, yielding a C‑index of 0.836-0.871, and enabled effective stratification for both DFS and overall survival (all log‑rank p < 0.01). Radiogenomic analysis revealed that high‑risk patients exhibited an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, elevated stromal scores, activated oncogenic pathways, and reduced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration.
CONCLUSION: IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients.
KEY POINTS: Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. Critical relevance statement High-risk patients stratified by the OP-PDAC model display a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, activation of core oncogenic signaling pathways, and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration.

items.title: Surufatinib and camrelizumab plus nab-paclitaxel-gemcitabine as first-line treatment for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surufatinib targets angiogenic and myeloid signaling pathways that may contribute to resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We evaluated surufatinib and camrelizumab added to nab-paclitaxel-gemcitabine (AG) in routine first-line treatment.
METHODS: This exploratory single-center retrospective cohort included 132 patients with metastatic PDAC and documented proficient mismatch repair or microsatellite stability who started first-line treatment during 2022-2025. Forty-four received surufatinib-camrelizumab plus AG and 88 received AG. Real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) was the primary outcome. Overall survival (OS), tumor response, safety, and treatment delivery were also assessed. Survival associations were adjusted for clinically selected baseline factors.
RESULTS: Median rwPFS was 6.3 months with the combination and 4.1 months with AG (log-rank P = 0.021); the adjusted hazard ratio was 0.73 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47-1.12; P = 0.152). Median OS was 9.7 versus 8.4 months (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.57-1.38). Unconfirmed objective response rates were 45.5% and 19.3%, respectively (P = 0.004). Confirmed response rates were 38.6% and 15.9% (P = 0.005). CA19-9 declined more in the combination group among patients with eligible paired measurements (P = 0.032). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 47.7% versus 34.1%, and toxicity-related permanent discontinuation occurred in 18.2% versus 11.4%. Median relative dose intensity was 87.0% versus 87.9% for both chemotherapy agents, 79.1% for prescribed surufatinib, and 100.0% for camrelizumab. Median follow-up by reverse Kaplan-Meier estimation was not estimable in either group.
CONCLUSION: Surufatinib-camrelizumab plus AG was associated with higher unconfirmed and confirmed response rates, without significant adjusted rwPFS or OS differences. The findings support prospective evaluation with attention to dose optimization and toxicity management.

items.title: KRAS and SKIL mutations synergistically promote pancreatic tumorigenesis through the ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation of Smad4.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer development requires oncogenic KRAS plus additional genetic hits, yet these cooperating events remain poorly defined. Starting from a germline SKIL A512T mutation discovered in an infant with IPMN, we explored the synergistic role of SKIL and KRAS in tumorigenesis.
METHODS: HEK293T cells with engineered SKIL A512T and/or KRAS G12V mutations were analyzed for proliferation, tumorigenicity, and signaling. Transcriptomics, ubiquitination assays, and protein interaction studies (Co-IP, immunofluorescence) delineated the mechanism.
RESULTS: SKIL normally protects Smad4 by binding its MH2 domain; SKIL loss exposes this domain to ubiquitination, but degradation occurs only when KRAS mutation upregulates the E3 ligase SMURF2. Clinically, a significant positive correlation was observed between SKIL and Smad4 protein expression in KRAS-mutant IPMN tissues.
CONCLUSION: We identify a novel synergy between SKIL loss and KRAS activation that drives pancreatic tumorigenesis through targeted Smad4 degradation. This study aids in identifying high-risk populations for pancreatic cancer, specifically those harboring KRAS mutations.

items.title: Real-world outcomes of serplulimab-based therapy in unresectable locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immunotherapy benefits many solid tumors, yet efficacy in pancreatic cancer (PC) remains limited given its immunologically cold phenotype. We evaluated the real-world effectiveness, safety, and treatment patterns of serplulimab-based regimens in unresectable locally advanced or metastatic PC.
METHODS: This two-center observational study retrospectively included adults with pathologically confirmed advanced PC who received serplulimab-based therapy as first- or later-line treatment. Short-term efficacy was assessed per RECIST v1.1, safety per CTCAE v5.0, and long-term benefit by overall survival (OS).
RESULTS: Among the 42 included patients, 24 received first-line (1 L) therapy and 18 received second-line or later (≥ 2 L) therapy. At a median follow-up of 17.7 months, the objective response rate (ORR) in the 1 L group was 25.0% (95% CI: 9.8-46.7%) and the disease control rate (DCR) was 83.3% (95% CI: 62.6-95.3%); in the ≥2 L group, the ORR was 22.2% (95% CI: 6.4-47.6%) and the DCR was 83.3% (95% CI: 58.6-96.4%). Median progression‑free survival was 6.2 months (95% CI: 4.4-9.3) in the 1 L group and 5.7 months (95% CI: 3.2-NR) in the ≥2 L group. Median OS was 10.3 months (95% CI: 8.0-12.9) in the 1 L group and 9.1 months (95% CI: 5.4-NR) in the ≥2 L group. Adverse events (AEs) occurred in 78.6%, predominantly hematologic; grade 3 or higher immune-related AEs occurred in 4.8%.
CONCLUSIONS: Serplulimab-based combinations showed preliminary antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile in advanced PC across both first-line and later-line settings. These real-world data generate hypotheses for larger, biomarker-integrated prospective studies to optimize combinations and improve the durability of benefit.

items.title: Oncogenic KRAS-MAPK signaling sustains a CD73 dependent therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is predominantly driven by oncogenic KRAS signaling and sustained by a desmoplastic, immunosuppressive microenvironment limiting therapeutic response. CD73-mediated adenosine signaling supports this immune-excluded, tumor-supportive microenvironment. Whether dual targeting of KRAS-MAPK and CD73 signaling creates a therapeutic opportunity to improve tumor control remains unexplored. Analysis of KRAS -mutant cancer cell lines revealed increased expression of NT5E and adenosine receptor ADORA2B . Pharmacologic and genetic suppression of oncogenic KRAS inhibited CD73 expression through a MAPK-dependent program. In syngeneic KPC tumors, conversely, CD73 inhibition with quemliclustat increased ERK phosphorylation in vivo , suggesting adaptive MAPK activation following CD73 blockade. Combined CD73 and RAS(ON) inhibition in vivo produced the strongest antitumor response, reducing endpoint tumor volume beyond either monotherapy. This combination significantly suppressed tumor proliferation and αSMA-positive stroma and resulted in a substantial reduction in CD163-positive macrophage infiltration. RAS-MAPK targeted therapy was also associated with increased CD8α-positive T cell infiltration and granzyme B-positive staining. As therapeutic responses in PDAC have been linked to the gut microbiome, we further examined treatment-associated changes in the microbiome. RAS-MAPK inhibition produced the most pronounced microbial alterations, which correlated with tumor volume and immune markers. Together, these findings identify KRAS–MAPK driven CD73 signaling as a therapeutic vulnerability in PDAC and support combined CD73 and RAS(ON) inhibition as a strategy to suppress tumor growth, remodel stroma, and alleviate tumor-associated immune suppression.

items.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

items.title: VOSE vs. MOSE in EUS-FNB for Pancreatic Masses
items.abstract: The primary endpoint of this study was to evaluate whether the histopathological diagnostic accuracy of VOSE EUS-FNB using 22-gauge (22G) Franseen or 22G Trident (Trident™) needles is non-inferior to that of MOSE EUS-FNB in pancreatic solid masses. The secondary endpoints included diagnostic sensitivity, diagnostic specificity, median number of needle passes, puncture time, and cytological diagnostic accuracy.

items.title: DNA Methylation-Based Testing for High Risk Populations
items.abstract: This study will study the feasibility of using multi-cancer early detection (MCED) testing in individuals at high risk for cancer development. We will look at participants to have germline mutations in cancer associated genes and participants who have pancreatic cysts. Participants will undergo testing and complete questionnaires to evaluating anxiety and adherence to standard screening after testing.

items.title: Association between close margin status and survival in the modern systemic treatment era for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The differential impact of negative resection margins that are > 1 mm (R0) or ≤ 1 mm (R0close) compared to positive (R1) margins on overall survival (OS) in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is unclear in the modern era of chemotherapy administration. Historically, R0close margins were shown to have a negative impact on OS compared to R0, but these data predate wide adoption of the current multiagent cytotoxic treatment regimens and neoadjuvant treatment approaches.
METHODS: We analyzed patients with PDAC undergoing pancreatectomy from April 2014 to April 2024 at a high-volume academic center. OS was assessed via Kaplan-Meier method, log-rank test, and Cox proportional hazard model to adjust for covariates.
RESULTS: A total of 514 pancreatectomies were identified. Of 256 patients with PDAC, margin assessment revealed R0, R0close, and R1 margins occurred in 62.9%, 29.3%, and 7.8% respectively. Overall, 93% of patients received systemic chemotherapy. Median OS was 48.6 months; 54.6 months for R0, 41.3 months for R0close, and 20.7 months for R1 (P = 0.04). The unadjusted Cox proportional hazard model did not show a significant difference in OS between R0 and R0close margins [hazard ratio (HR) = 1.16, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.80-1.69] but showed a significant difference in OS between R0 and R1 margins (R1: HR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.16-3.60). The results of the adjusted model incorporating demographic, surgical, and clinicopathologic variables were similar (R0close: HR = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.71-1.67; R1: HR = 1.88, 95% CI: 1.01-3.52).
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients undergoing resection for PDAC and treated with multiagent systemic therapy, survival linearly decreased with R0, R0close, and R1 status, with no significant difference between R0 and R0close margins.

items.title: Factors associated with mood and anxiety disorders in patients with cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mood and anxiety disorders are common in cancer survivors, and are associated with worse outcomes; however, systematic identification of high-risk patients remains limited, despite screening and intervention guidelines. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to identify risk factors for mood and anxiety disorders, including diagnoses and clinically significant symptoms, in adult cancer survivors.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for cohort and case-control studies published from January 2000 to November 2024 that evaluated cancer-related, sociodemographic, lifestyle, and psychosocial risk factors in adults with breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, stomach, liver, or pancreatic cancer. Random-effects models with robust variance estimation pooled relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for factors assessed in ≥5 studies.
RESULTS: Fifty of the 53 eligible studies were included in the meta-analysis. Consistent risk factors included high tumor stage (vs. low; n = 28; RR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.21-1.97), more physical comorbidities (vs. fewer; n = 36; RR, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.34-1.84), prior psychiatric history (high vs. low burden; n = 13; RR, 4.85; 95% CI, 2.77-8.50), female sex (vs. male; n = 19; RR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.32-1.75), underweight body mass index (vs. normal; n = 6; RR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.55-2.44), unmarried status (vs. married; n = 25; RR, 1.35; 95% CI, 1.14-1.58), and current smoking (vs. never; n = 12; RR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.12-1.46). Suggestive associations, although less consistent in sensitivity analyses, were observed for high tumor grade, more extensive surgery, low income, low education, and low social support.
CONCLUSIONS: Several clinical and social factors were associated with increased risk of mood and anxiety outcomes in adult cancer survivors. These findings may support risk-based psychiatric screening and early intervention in resource-limited oncology settings.

items.title: Incremental Prognostic Value of the Preoperative Controlling Nutritional Status Score in Patients Undergoing Surgery for Resectable Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score is a prognostic marker in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but its incremental value beyond conventional preoperative factors and its performance relative to other immunonutritional or inflammatory indices remain unclear. We evaluated the prognostic significance and incremental value of the preoperative CONUT score in resectable PDAC.
METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included 287 patients with resectable PDAC undergoing curative-intent pancreatectomy. Patients were stratified by preoperative CONUT score (0-1, 2-4, or ≥ 5). Overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) were analyzed using Cox models with preoperative factors. Recurrence was evaluated using Gray's test and Fine-Gray regression, with death before recurrence as a competing event. For model comparison, the CONUT score and other immunonutritional or inflammatory indices were added separately to the preoperative base model and evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), Akaike information criterion (AIC), and likelihood ratio test.
RESULTS: Five-year OS was 51.5%, 31.5%, and 18.6% for CONUT scores of 0-1, 2-4, and ≥ 5, respectively (p < 0.001). Higher CONUT categories were independently associated with worse OS (2-4, hazard ratio [HR] 1.604, p = 0.007; ≥ 5, HR 2.410, p < 0.001). Five-year RFS was 42.6%, 23.2%, and 17.4%, respectively (p < 0.001); higher CONUT categories remained independently associated with worse RFS (2-4, HR 1.543, p = 0.008; ≥ 5, HR 2.006, p = 0.002). Recurrence incidence increased with higher CONUT scores (Gray's test, p = 0.006). A high CONUT score (≥ 5) was independently associated with increased recurrence risk (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.780; p = 0.022). Adding the CONUT score to the base model improved fit (C-index, 0.629; AIC, 1802.53; likelihood ratio test, p < 0.001). The prognostic nutritional index (PNI) also improved fit, with modest differences versus the CONUT score.
CONCLUSIONS: The preoperative CONUT score was independently associated with OS and RFS after surgery for resectable PDAC and provided modest incremental prognostic information beyond conventional preoperative factors. A high CONUT score was associated with increased recurrence risk. These findings suggest that the CONUT score may help refine preoperative risk stratification.

items.title: Mesopancreas Excision in Pancreaticoduodenectomy for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
items.abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer, is treated when it arises in the head of the pancreas and can be removed by an operation called pancreaticoduodenectomy (the Whipple operation), followed by chemotherapy. Even after this operation the cancer returns in most patients. One important reason is that microscopic cancer cells are often left at the cut edges of the removed tissue, especially at the edge facing the superior mesenteric artery, the main artery that supplies the intestine. The tissue in this area, behind the head of the pancreas, is called the mesopancreas. It contains fat, lymph vessels, lymph nodes and nerves, through which pancreatic cancer commonly spreads.

Total mesopancreas excision is a refinement of the standard operation. The surgeon removes the whole mesopancreas in one piece together with the head of the pancreas by dissecting directly along the right side of the superior mesenteric artery, in the same way that the whole fatty envelope of the rectum is removed in rectal cancer surgery. Studies that compared patients operated on with and without this technique suggest that it may leave fewer cancer cells behind and reduce the chance of the cancer returning in the operated area, without increasing complications. Those studies were not randomized, however, so it is still unknown whether the technique itself is responsible for these benefits.

In this single-center randomized controlled trial, 110 adults with removable (resectable) cancer of the head of the pancreas will be assigned by chance, during the operation and after the surgeon has confirmed that the tumor can be removed, to pancreaticoduodenectomy with total mesopancreas excision or to standard pancreaticoduodenectomy. Patients, and the doctors who examine the removed tissue and the follow-up scans, will not be told which operation was performed. The main question is whether total mesopancreas excision increases the proportion of patients in whom no cancer cells are found within 1 mm of any cut edge (an R0 resection). The trial will also compare complications, diarrhea, recovery, the number of lymph nodes removed, the chance and pattern of cancer recurrence, survival and quality of life over 2 years of follow-up.

items.title: Preoperative CA 19-9 and the Pattern and Timing of Recurrence After Pancreatoduodenectomy (Whipple Operation) for Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
Surgery to remove the head of the pancreas (pancreatoduodenectomy, also called the Whipple operation), usually followed by chemotherapy, is the only treatment that offers long-term survival for cancer in the head of the pancreas (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma). Even so, the cancer comes back (recurs) in most patients. Where it comes back first (around the operation site, in the liver, in the lining of the abdomen, in the lungs or elsewhere) and how soon it comes back both affect survival, the choice of further treatment and how patients should be followed up.

CA 19-9 is a blood test measured routinely before this operation. A high level is known to be linked with shorter survival, but whether it also predicts where and when the cancer will recur is uncertain and, to the investigator's knowledge, has not been studied in patients treated in Egypt. Jaundice, which is common in these patients, can raise CA 19-9 falsely, so this study uses only CA 19-9 values measured when the blood bilirubin level was close to normal (2 mg/dL or less).

This is a retrospective study of existing medical records. It includes adults who had a Whipple operation for this cancer at the Hepatopancreatobiliary and Surgical Oncology Unit, Liver and GIT Hospital, Minia University, Egypt, between January 2017 and December 2024, with follow-up information from Minia Oncology Centre. No patient will receive any test or treatment for the study, and no care will be changed. Patients will be compared according to their preoperative CA 19-9 level (37 U/mL or less versus more than 37 U/mL).

The two main questions are whether the preoperative CA 19-9 level is linked to (1) the site of the first recurrence and (2) the time from surgery to recurrence. A recurrence will count only when confirmed by scans or biopsy, never by a rising CA 19-9 alone, and it will be classified by independent doctors who do not know the patients' CA 19-9 results. Other questions include recurrence within 6 and 12 months of surgery, survival, and whether CA 19-9 adds useful information to the routine findings available before surgery.

The investigator expects that patients with a high CA 19-9 will more often recur first in the liver or the lining of the abdomen and will recur sooner, whereas patients with a normal level will recur later and more often only near the operation site. The findings may help tailor follow-up after surgery, identify patients who might benefit from chemotherapy before surgery, and identify patients whose cancer is likely to come back only at the operation site, who might be considered for further local treatment.

items.title: Early detection and interception in hepato-pancreatic-biliary cancers: endoscopic imaging, liquid biopsy, and emerging molecular biomarkers.
items.abstract: Early detection of hepato-pancreatic-biliary cancers requires different strategies because the populations at risk, precursor lesions, and accessible specimens vary by organ. This review examines established endoscopic imaging and tissue-acquisition pathways together with circulating and lesion-derived biomarkers. Inherited or familial pancreatic risk defines the main pancreatic surveillance population; endoscopic ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging are complementary, and prospective cohorts show a stage shift but also interval cancers and low-yield surgery. In pancreatic cysts, imaging features and selective tissue or cyst-fluid analysis can refine management, but no fluid marker independently identifies high-grade dysplasia with sufficient certainty. For biliary cancer, surveillance in primary sclerosing cholangitis depends on noninvasive imaging, whereas endoscopic ductal sampling, cholangioscopy-guided biopsy, and selective endoscopic ultrasonography address suspicious strictures; bile methylation and sequencing may increase diagnostic yield when an invasive procedure is already indicated. Endoscopy has a selective role in gallbladder lesions and a direct interception role in histologically confirmed ampullary adenomas. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance remains based on ultrasonography with alpha-fetoprotein; cell-free DNA methylation and multi-analyte blood tests are promising but have not replaced guideline-based surveillance. Across organs, case-control accuracy does not establish surveillance utility. Liquid biopsy complements rather than generally replaces histopathological diagnosis. Established adjuncts must be distinguished from investigational assays, including those with prospective diagnostic validation but no demonstrated surveillance utility. Integration requires specimen-specific analytical validation, independent testing in the intended-use population, and evidence of incremental clinical value over standard imaging and endoscopy. Interventional studies must show that this approach reduces late-stage diagnosis without excessive false-positive procedures.

items.title: Tumor location in the pancreatic body/tail as an independent risk factor for early recurrence after curative resection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a single-center retrospective study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early recurrence after radical resection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a primary cause of poor prognosis. Published definitions of early recurrence use postoperative cutoff points ranging from 6 to 12 months. This study aimed to analyze perioperative clinicopathological features associated with early recurrence after PDAC surgery, with particular focus on the impact of tumor location, to facilitate individualized treatment decisions.
METHODS: Clinical data from 155 patients with PDAC who underwent pancreatectomy at Panjin Liao-Oil Field Gem Flower Hospital between January 2011 and December 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. In this study, early recurrence was defined as recurrence within 6 months after surgery. Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test was used to evaluate survival outcomes. Two separate multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to identify independent predictors of early recurrence: one including preoperative variables and one including postoperative variables. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported for these logistic regression models.
RESULTS: The R0 resection rate was significantly higher for pancreatic body/tail tumors than for head/neck tumors (P = 0.040). Among 155 patients, 55 (35.5%) developed recurrence within 6 months (early recurrence group), 78 (50.3%) had non-early recurrence, and 22 (14.2%) showed no recurrence. The early recurrence group had a significantly higher proportion of multiple-organ metastasis (P = 0.019) and significantly shorter overall survival (P < 0.001). No significant differences in recurrence patterns or overall survival were observed between tumor location subgroups (P > 0.05). In the preoperative multivariable model, only CA19-9 ≥ 208 IU/mL was an independent predictor of early recurrence (P = 0.021); body/tail location was not statistically significant (P = 0.123). In the postoperative multivariable model, body/tail tumor location, tumor size ≥ 3.3 cm (based on postoperative pathological measurement), TNM stage III, and lack of postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy were independent risk factors for recurrence within 6 months (P < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center retrospective cohort, body/tail tumor location was associated with early recurrence within 6 months after curative-intent PDAC surgery in the postoperative multivariable model, but it was not independently significant in the preoperative model and did not significantly affect overall survival. This finding is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation. Incorporating tumor location into preoperative risk stratification may warrant prospective evaluation as one component of a preoperative risk model.

items.title: Mesentericoportal Venous Shunting in Surgery for Locally Advanced Pancreatic Tumors: Results of a Standardized Approach for Oncovascular Pancreatic Surgery.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgery for locally advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (LA-PDAC) remains technically demanding, particularly in presence of extensive venous involvement. A temporary mesenterico-portal shunt (TMPS) facilitates long venous resection and enables safe arterial resection, but evidence is limited to small series. We report technique and outcomes from the largest cohort of TMPS, an approach described at our center.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: All pancreatic resections performed with TMPS between January 2007 and December 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Operative and survival outcomes were analyzed.
RESULTS: 155 LA-PDAC patients underwent TMPS placement. Most had LA-PDAC (92%) and received preoperative chemotherapy (89%), mainly FOLFIRINOX-based (86.9%). Complete venous obstruction (Nakao D) was present in 48.1%. Procedures included pancreatoduodenectomy (62%), total (24.5%), and distal pancreatectomy (13.5%). All patients underwent venous resection; 75% also required arterial resection, most commonly of the superior mesenteric artery (61%). Mean operative time was 610 min (range 180-1145 min). Postoperative mortality was 6.4%, and R0 resection was achieved in 56%. The median OS from diagnosis was 32.7 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 23.5-42.00 months).The median OS from surgery was 17.46 months (95% CI 13.2-21.6 months), with 1-, 3, and 5-year survival rates of 70%, 29%, and 21%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: TMPS is a standardized and reproducible technique that facilitates management of complex venous resection and may enhance the feasibility of arterial resection in selected patients with LA-PDAC.

items.title: A genetically engineered porcine model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma captures the biological complexity of the human disease
items.abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive cancer with limited treatment options and poor patient outcomes. The lack of clinically relevant large animal models hinders the investigation of early disease mechanisms and translational therapeutic strategies. In this study, we present a genetically engineered porcine PDAC model involving pancreas-specific activation of latent KRAS G12D alone (KC) or in combination with TP53 R 167 H (KPC), developed in a midipig background. KC pigs predominantly developed progressive acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM), whereas KPC pigs showed accelerated tumour progression, including PanINs, invasive carcinoma, perineural invasion, and early lymphatic dissemination. Histopathological and molecular analyses revealed pronounced intra- and inter-tumour heterogeneity, a complex stromal microenvironment, and expression of key PDAC markers. Tumours exhibited early alterations in oncogenic KRAS signalling, including increased dosage and differential expression of isoforms, together with dysregulation of tumour suppressor networks involving p16 and TP53 family members. Single-cell transcriptomics and flow cytometric analyses demonstrated an organised and functionally active immune landscape in early lesions, characterised by infiltrating effector and regulatory T-cell populations. Porcine pancreatic cancer cell lines (PoPaCa) were established from KC and KPC tumours, recapitulating key genetic and transcriptional features of the primary lesions. Exploratory drug screening demonstrated heterogeneous responses to clinically relevant and experimental compounds. Responses to gemcitabine and paclitaxel overlapped qualitatively with those observed in human PDAC cell lines, whereas pronounced sensitivity to the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3 and partial responsiveness to trametinib identified testable therapeutic phenotypes for further validation. Together, this genetically engineered porcine PDAC model captures early molecular, cellular, and microenvironmental features of pancreatic tumorigenesis and provides a translational platform to study disease initiation, tumour heterogeneity, immune interactions, and therapeutic response beyond the constraints of rodent models.

Graphical abstract

Pancreas-specific activation of mutant KRAS and TP53 in genetically engineered pigs recapitulates key features of human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and provides a platform for studying tumour biology, biomarkers and therapeutic responses.

items.title: The imPAct of nutritioN on the Outcome of pancrEATic Surgery; Food for Thought.
items.abstract:
Patients with cancer or chronic inflammatory disorders, such as periampullary malignancies or chronic pancreatitis (CP), often experience severe weight loss and a progressive decline in health and functional performance. These changes result from a complex interaction between the disease and the host, affecting multiple physiological factors. However, in daily clinical practice the focus is predominantly placed on treatment of the disorder itself, whereas less attention is given to the physical condition of the patient before treatment commences. Factors such as malnutrition, reduced aerobic fitness, and adverse body composition have all been associated with worse outcomes, including a higher risk of postoperative complications or inability to complete oncological treatment.

The central hypothesis of the investigators is that improving the patient's overall condition before treatment, particularly before major surgery, will enhance treatment tolerance, reduce complications, and improve overall quality of life (QoL). Among the various modifiable factors in the disease-host interaction, nutritional status occupies a central role, directly influencing muscle mass and strength, immune competence, metabolic stability, and recovery capacity.

items.title: PHGDH Inhibition Confers a Targetable Glutamine Dependency in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) develops in a nutrient-poor microenvironment and progresses from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) to invasive carcinoma. Serine metabolism supports tumor growth in many cancers, spurring the development of inhibitors of phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), the rate-limiting enzyme in serine biosynthesis. However, the limited clinical success of PHGDH inhibitors highlights the need to better understand the stage-specific role of de novo serine synthesis during PDAC progression. Here, we showed that PHGDH increases progressively from PanIN to invasive PDAC in human and mouse tissues. In genetically engineered mouse models with inducible PHGDH knockdown, PHGDH loss delayed PDAC development. Acute treatment with the PHGDH inhibitor BI-9593 suppressed de novo serine synthesis, induced cell death, and drove tumor regression. Unexpectedly, PHGDH-deficient tumors did not become more dependent on exogenous serine, and dietary serine/glycine manipulation did not affect tumor development. Instead, stable isotope tracing and metabolomic profiling showed that PHGDH loss reduced ASCT2 expression and impaired glutamine uptake and utilization, creating a metabolic liability that rendered PHGDH-deficient tumors selectively sensitive to the glutamine antagonist DRP-104. Together, these findings reveal a therapeutic vulnerability to combined metabolic targeting in PDAC.
