Quo vadis? - Visualizing the tropism of tumor-derived cellular nanovesicles.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and nanovesicles (NVs) derived from tumor cells hold great potential for targeted drug delivery due to their inherent tumor-homing properties.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the physicochemical characteristics, cellular uptake, pharmacokinetics, tumor accumulation, and biodistribution of sEVs and NVs derived from two different cancer cell lines.
METHODS: sEVs and NVs were isolated from human metastatic breast cancer (MDA231) and pancreatic cancer (8988t) cells, respectively, and then characterized, further labeled with PbS quantum dots (QDs) or PKH26 dye. Cellular uptake of sEVs from different parental cells was examined by MDA231 cells in vitro, and in vivo biodistribution and pharmacokinetics of different sEVs and NVs were assessed in MDA231 cell-xenografted mouse models, tracked under fluorescence imaging in the visible or near-infrared (NIR) II region.
RESULTS: Having comparable particle sizes and surface charges, MDA231-derived sEVs exhibited preferential uptake by MDA231 cells compared with sEVs derived from 8988t cells. In contrast, NVs showed a higher level of CD9 tetraspanin inheritance than sEVs when normalized to the total protein input of the same parental cell. In vivo fluorescence imaging revealed similar circulation half-lives of approximately 4-5 h for both MDA231- and 8988t-derived sEVs and NVs. PbS QD labeling provided stronger and more stable fluorescence signals than PKH26 dye. MDA231-derived sEVs or NVs showed higher accumulation in MDA231 tumor-bearing mice than their counterparts originating from 8988t cells.
CONCLUSION: Tumor-derived sEVs and NVs exhibit favorable pharmacokinetic profiles and enhanced accumulation in homologous tumors, underscoring their promise as targeted delivery platforms for cancer therapy.

items.title: β-hydroxybutyrate and cancer: an update on conflicting roles and therapeutic targeting.
items.abstract: Cancer metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of malignancy, within which ketone body metabolism, particularly β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), has garnered significant attention due to its complex and paradoxical roles in tumor biology. This review systematically examines the multifaceted functions of BHB in cancer, spanning molecular mechanisms to clinical translation, and synthesizes the conflicting evidence regarding its tumor-suppressive and tumor-promoting effects. We first explore the potential of BHB as a diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive biomarker, where its differential abundance across cancers such as colorectal and pancreatic cancer underscores its context-dependent nature. We then examine the underlying molecular mechanisms that account for these opposing effects. A key focus of this review is the integration of recent advances in combination therapies involving BHB alongside chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and physical treatments, highlighting its emerging potential as a promising sensitizer for combination regimens. Finally, we systematically outline the core controversies and challenges in the field, attributing the diversity of BHB effects to heterogeneity in tumor metabolic phenotypes, molecular subtypes, and the tumor microenvironment. By constructing a framework that integrates mechanistic diversity, clinical evidence, and combination therapeutic strategies, this review underscores the imperative to shift from a "one-size-fits-all" paradigm toward precision stratification based on tumor metabolic phenotypes, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the development of safe and effective BHB/ketogenic diet-based combination therapies.

items.title: GLUD1 mediates leucine signaling to restrain POLRMT proteolysis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis.
items.abstract: Mitochondria maintain unique biogenesis programs (mitobiogenesis) to encode key components in oxidative phosphorylation system in response to metabolic cues. How mitochondria integrate specific metabolite signals into mitobiogenesis remains elusive. Here, we report that pancreatic cancer cells employ glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (GLUD1) to couple leucine signaling and mitobiogenesis. Mitochondrial RNA polymerase (POLRMT) positively correlates with GLUD1 at proteomic level, but not transcriptomic level, in cancer cell lines. GLUD1 maintains POLRMT protein, mitochondrial genome (mtDNA)-encoded protein expression, and mitochondrial mass independent of its catalytic activity. Notably, GLUD1 interacts with POLRMT and protects it from caspase 9 (CASP9)-mediated proteolysis. Metabolite screening reveals that leucine, an abundant amino acid in mtDNA-encoded proteins, enhances GLUD1 binding to stabilize POLRMT. Depletion of solute carrier family 25 member 44 (SLC25A44), the mitochondrial leucine transporter, reduces POLRMT protein and suppresses mitobiogenesis. GLUD1-mediated leucine signaling supports mitochondrial respiration and pancreatic cancer cell growth in culture and in vivo. Clinical pancreatic tumor tissues accumulate leucine and upregulate GLUD1, which is linked to enhanced mitobiogenesis. Together, GLUD1 mediates leucine signaling to support mitobiogenesis and pancreatic cancer development.

items.title: Advanced Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma With Complete Response to Chemoimmunotherapy: A Case Report and Single-Cell Profiling.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has a poor prognosis, especially in unresectable disease. We report a patient with metastatic PDAC who achieved durable complete remission after PD-1 blockade combined with gemcitabine and albumin-bound paclitaxel and remains disease-free 4 years after diagnosis. To explore the immune basis of this response, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from seven patients receiving the same regimen. Responders showed enrichment of terminally differentiated CD8+ T (Temra) and CD4 ISG+ T helper (Th) cells compared with nonresponders. Across independent cohorts, these two programs were positively correlated, suggesting coordinated immune activation during effective therapy. Predicted ligand-target interactions were linked to cytotoxic and immune activation pathways. These findings suggest that coordinated expansion of CD4+ ISG+ Th and CD8+ Temra cells are associated with durable chemoimmunotherapy responses in PDAC and support peripheral blood immune profiling as a minimally invasive monitoring strategy. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05201729.

items.title: Cancer risk with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists: An umbrella review of meta-analyses.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) for diabetes and obesity is increasing, but effects on uncommon or long-latency cancers are uncertain. We synthesised meta-analytic evidence for overall and site-specific cancer risk and assessed methodological quality, overlap, outcome-level certainty, and credibility.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 30 June 2026 for meta-analyses of GLP-1RAs or the dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide and incident cancer. Randomised and observational evidence was considered separately; review-level estimates were not recombined. We assessed methodological confidence with AMSTAR 2, overlap with corrected covered area (CCA), outcome-level certainty with a GRADE-informed algorithm, and association credibility with Ioannidis criteria.
FINDINGS: We included 38 meta-analyses from 2012 to 2026. The most comprehensive placebo-controlled randomised evidence (48 trials, 94 245 participants, median follow-up 70 weeks) showed no statistically significant association with thyroid cancer (odds ratio [OR] 1·37, 95% CI 0·82-2·31; 1 fewer to 9 more cases per 10 000 treated), pancreatic cancer (0·84, 0·53-1·35), colorectal cancer (1·11, 0·75-1·65), or breast cancer (0·95, 0·60-1·49), and no overall cancer increase (OR 1·05, 0·98-1·13 across 50 trials). Thyroid and agent-specific haematological signals were inconsistent or based on sparse events; between-review discordance for thyroid and colorectal cancer was largely attributable to comparator restriction, choice of estimator, and handling of zero-event trials rather than to differences in cancer ascertainment. Observational syntheses suggested lower hepatocellular carcinoma risk (hazard ratio 0·60, 95% CI 0·41-0·88), but four reviews had very high overlap (CCA 50·0%). Outcome-level certainty was moderate for five outcomes, low for 11, and very low for five; none was high. No association met class I or II credibility criteria.
INTERPRETATION: Randomised evidence shows no evidence of a material increase in overall or site-specific cancer risk over currently observed trial durations (median about 70 weeks, maximum about 5 years), and cancer concerns alone do not justify withholding indicated GLP-1RA treatment. Small, rare, long-latency, dose-specific, or agent-specific effects cannot be excluded, and the evidence cannot address exposure beyond approximately five years, well short of the 8-10 years generally required to evaluate cancer incidence. Observational protective associations should not support causal or cancer-prevention claims.
FUNDING: None.

items.title: SMAD4 loss drives cancer chromosomal instability through transcription-replication conflict-associated replication stress.
items.abstract: Cancer chromosomal instability (CIN) drives tumor evolution through generating structural and numerical chromosome aberrations. However, its molecular determinants remain poorly characterized. Here, we uncover a yet unrecognized role for the tumor suppressor SMAD4 as a key regulator of chromosomal stability. Mechanistically, loss of SMAD4 causes replication stress by promoting transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs) and induces subsequent mitotic errors, leading to the concomitant emergence of structural and numerical CIN. While the tumor suppressor function of SMAD4 has been predominantly attributed to transforming growth factor-β signaling, we find that its role in genome maintenance operates via bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling and its transcriptional target gene ID3. Consequently, inhibition of BMP signaling mimics the loss of SMAD4, while reexpression of SMAD4 or ID3 in SMAD4-deficient colorectal or pancreatic cancer cells suppresses TRCs, replication stress, and mitotic errors. Our findings reveal a TRC- and replication stress-driven mechanism by which loss of BMP-SMAD4 signaling causes cancer CIN.

items.title: Engrailed-1: a context-dependent regulator of development, fibroblast plasticity, fibrosis, and cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The homeodomain transcription factor Engrailed-1 (EN1) is best known for its roles in developmental patterning and the maintenance of neuronal integrity. Recent studies indicate that EN1 can be reactivated under pathological stress, where it contributes to fibroblast state transitions, fibrotic remodeling, and selected cancer phenotypes. In this review, we integrate the diverse biological roles of EN1 across embryonic development, tissue regeneration, fibrosis, and oncogenesis. We distinguish correlative expression patterns from causal evidence and incorporate recent insights from single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies.
MAIN FINDINGS: In the skin, fibroblasts with an EN1 lineage history have a strong propensity for scar formation. Injury-associated mechanical tension can also induce EN1 expression in previously EN1-negative fibroblasts through a YAP-dependent mechanism. TGF-β/SMAD3 signaling provides an additional route to EN1 induction and links EN1 to cytoskeletal remodeling, ROCK activity, and myofibroblast differentiation. Studies using targeted siRNA delivery indicate that this profibrotic program is at least partly reversible. In cancer, the strongest functional evidence for EN1 involvement comes from basal-like breast cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, glioma, and adenoid cystic carcinoma, although the downstream consequences are highly dependent on cellular context.
CONCLUSION: EN1 is better viewed as a context-dependent regulator of cell state than as a universal oncogene or a generic fibrosis marker. Therapeutic targeting of EN1 will therefore require cell-specific delivery, well-defined direct regulatory networks, and careful assessment of on-target adverse effects.
items.venue: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

items.title: Rapidly enlarging pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with discordant multimodality treatment response.
items.abstract: Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (ACC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor whose imaging appearance can overlap with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and other solid pancreatic neoplasms. We report a man in his 50's with a pancreatic head mass causing biliary and pancreatic ductal obstruction. A noncontrast computed tomography (CT) performed approximately 10 months earlier, retrospectively reviewed, showed a small pancreatic head lesion without secondary signs of malignancy, which subsequently enlarged to approximately 8 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large expansile heterogeneous mass with prominent enhancement and extensive central necrosis, initially raising concern for PDAC but prompting consideration of ACC, which was confirmed by endoscopic biopsy with immunohistochemistry. Surgical resection was initially considered, but the patient repeatedly declined surgery, and systemic chemotherapy was given after biliary decompression. Follow-up CT showed near-complete morphological resolution of the mass, whereas FDG-PET/CT showed persistent focal uptake (SUVmax 6.2) and MRI showed a residual diffusion-restricting lesion. The patient was subsequently persuaded to proceed to surgery and underwent a Whipple procedure; histopathology confirmed residual acinar cell carcinoma with clear margins and no nodal metastases, indicating that the CT response had underestimated persistent disease. This case highlights the value of reviewing prior imaging for interval growth, recognizing atypical imaging features of a pancreatic head mass, and integrating CT, PET/CT, magnetic resonance imaging and, when feasible, pathological confirmation when assessing treatment response.

items.title: Statement of Retraction: CDC25C is a prognostic biomarker and correlated with mitochondrial homeostasis in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
Biomarker testing in tumours of the digestive system.
items.abstract: Precision oncology has profoundly transformed the management of digestive malignancies, making predictive biomarker testing an integral component of routine pathology practice. Beyond identifying actionable molecular alterations, pathologists now face the challenge of selecting appropriate testing strategies, preserving limited tissue, ensuring analytical quality and integrating increasingly complex biomarker data into multidisciplinary therapeutic decision-making. This review provides a practical overview of clinically actionable biomarker testing across digestive cancers, focusing on current testing strategies, methodological challenges and tumour-specific applications. We discuss the complementary roles of immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridisation and molecular techniques, together with practical aspects of tissue stewardship, pre-analytical optimisation, tumour heterogeneity and biomarker re-testing. Particular emphasis is placed on integrating predictive biomarkers into routine diagnostic workflows while maintaining analytical robustness and clinical relevance. Current biomarker requirements are reviewed across the major digestive tumour types, including upper gastrointestinal, colorectal, small bowel, hepatocellular, biliary and pancreatic cancer, as well as gastrointestinal stromal tumours, highlighting both organ-specific biomarkers and emerging tumour-agnostic approaches. The review also addresses contemporary frameworks for clinical actionability, multidisciplinary interpretation of molecular findings and future developments, including comprehensive genomic profiling, liquid biopsy, digital pathology and artificial intelligence. By integrating methodological principles with tumour-specific applications, this review highlights the central role of the pathologist in delivering high-quality precision oncology and provides practical guidance for implementing predictive biomarker testing in routine clinical practice.
items.venue: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology

items.title: Extracellular vesicle surface glycosylation in clinical chemistry: Biological mechanisms, analytical challenges, and translational evidence.
items.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) expose a glycocalyx that integrates cellular glycosylation programs with vesicle biogenesis, trafficking and interactions in biofluids. This surface layer is analytically attractive because it can be interrogated on intact particles and can encode disease-associated changes in sialylation, fucosylation, N-glycan branching, high-mannose structures and mucin-type O-glycans. Human studies, particularly in pancreatic cancer and lung or breast cancer, have converted selected EV-associated glycan motifs into measurable liquid-biopsy signals, whereas evidence in other diseases remains preliminary. Translation remains constrained by an unresolved measurand problem: EV abundance, glycan density, carrier identity, isolation selectivity, lipoprotein contamination and affinity avidity can each change the observed signal. This review integrates the biological architecture of the EV glycocalyx with the analytical workflow required for clinical chemistry. It compares affinity, mass-spectrometric and single-EV approaches; evaluates disease-specific evidence; and defines pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical sources of variation. A translational framework is proposed in which candidate EV glycan biomarkers progress from structural and mechanistic confirmation through intended-use assay design, analytical validation, independent clinical validation and multicenter implementation. EV glycosylation is positioned not as another untargeted omics layer but as a surface-accessible signal defined by the vesicle population and assay whose value depends on explicit definition of the vesicle population and glycan measurand.
items.venue: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry

items.title: Current perspectives of CAR-T cells therapy in peritoneal carcinomatosis.
items.abstract: Peritoneal carcinomatosis (PC) is a frequent pattern of tumor dissemination across multiple malignancies, including colorectal, gastric, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers, and is associated with poor prognosis and limited survival. Although cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with or without hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) has improved outcomes in selected patients, its indication remains restricted, leaving a substantial proportion of patients without curative options, and recurrence rates remain high even after treatment. Therefore, the development of novel therapeutic strategies is urgently needed. Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising approach, achieving remarkable success in hematological malignancies and gaining increasing attention in solid tumors. Several tumor-associated antigens, including CEA, CLDN18.2, GUCY2C, EpCAM, and mesothelin, have been investigated across different tumor types, showing encouraging preclinical and early clinical results. In particular, similar to HIPEC, regional delivery strategies such as intraperitoneal administration may enhance tumor targeting, improve cell trafficking, and increase therapeutic efficacy in peritoneal disease. However, CAR-T cell therapy in PC faces important challenges inherent to solid tumors, including antigen heterogeneity, limited tumor trafficking and infiltration, and a hostile tumor microenvironment characterized by dense stromal barriers and immunosuppressive conditions, which ultimately limit its efficacy. Overcoming these barriers is essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review summarizes the current evidence on CAR-T cell therapy in major solid tumors associated with PC, highlighting key targets, administration strategies, and clinical outcomes, while addressing the main limitations and emerging strategies to improve its clinical application, as well as future perspectives for its integration into multimodal treatment approaches.

items.title: Progress in anticancer chemical constituents and pharmacological research of Carpesium cernuum L. (Review).
items.abstract: The present study aimed to systematically review the anticancer chemical constituents, pharmacological effects, and molecular targets of Carpesium cernuum L., clarify the molecular network of its anticancer mechanisms, summarize the research achievements and limitations and provide a scientific reference for its development and utilization, the research and development of novel anticancer drugs, and clinical applications. Through literature collation and experimental data integration, the chemical constituents of C. cernuum were classified and identified, and with the aid of in vitro cell experiments, partial in vivo animal experiments and molecular biology techniques, the anticancer effects of its extracts and active constituents as well as the key signaling pathways were investigated. Notably, all included evidence was strictly stratified by research type (crude extract/fraction/isolated monomer, in vitro cell model/in vivo animal model/network pharmacology prediction) to clarify the evidence level of each anticancer claim. A total of 109 compounds were isolated and identified from C. cernuum, among which 60 sesquiterpenoids were the major components. Its active constituents exhibited promising inhibitory effects in preclinical studies against multiple cancers including prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, leukemia and breast cancer. Existing anticancer evidence was predominantly derived from in vitro cell-based assays, with a small number of in vivo animal validations and preliminary network pharmacology predictions; high-level clinical evidence is still vacant. By regulating signaling pathways such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt/mTOR and Hippo, they exert multi-dimensional anticancer effects, including cell proliferation inhibition, apoptosis induction, and metastasis suppression. In vitro and partial in vivo preclinical evidence indicates that the active ingredients of C. cernuum exert potential inhibitory effects against various tumors such as prostate cancer and pancreatic cancer. By targeting key signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt/mTOR and Hippo, it achieves multi-modal anticancer effects such as proliferation inhibition and apoptosis induction, showing favorable preliminary biocompatibility in existing preclinical experiments. However, the current research has limitations including insufficient in vivo verification, uneven evidence quality, and lack of standardized dose-effect data, which restrict clinical transformation. Collectively, C. cernuum and its bio-active metabolites display pre-clinical antitumor potential, yet further pharmacological validation and translational investigations are required to evaluate clinical applicability.

items.title: Single-session endoscopic repair of an iatrogenic esophageal perforation and endoscopic ultrasound-guided biliary drainage in a patient presenting with distal malignant biliary obstruction.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Esophageal perforation is a rare but serious adverse event of upper endoscopy. Advances in endoscopic closure now permit nonoperative management in selected cases. We describe a single-session approach combining endoscopic repair of a large esophageal perforation with EUS-guided biliary drainage in a frail patient with malignant biliary obstruction.
METHODS: An 88-year-old woman undergoing EUS for obstructive jaundice was found to have a 3- to 4-cm full-thickness midesophageal perforation with mediastinal communication. After multidisciplinary evaluation, primary endoscopic closure was performed using full-thickness over-the-scope suturing. Closure integrity was assessed with fluoroscopic contrast injection. This was followed by reinforcement with a through-the-scope helical tack suturing system. Given the patient's stability and confirmed repair, same-session EUS-guided biliary drainage was attempted. EUS-guided choledochoduodenostomy with placement of a lumen-apposing metal stent resulted in immediate biliary drainage.
RESULTS: Postprocedural interval imaging demonstrated no esophageal leak, and total bilirubin improved from 14 mg/dL to 2.5 mg/dL by discharge. Cytology confirmed pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
CONCLUSIONS: This case demonstrates that prompt endoscopic repair of a large esophageal perforation using suturing and tack-based reinforcement can permit safe same-session continuation of EUS-guided biliary drainage in carefully selected high-risk patients.
items.venue: VideoGIE : an official video journal of the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

items.title: Small molecule inhibitors targeting METTL3 in cancer: Preclinical and clinical advances, combination strategies.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most prevalent epitranscriptomic modification in eukaryotic mRNA, precisely regulating RNA splicing, stability, and translation. Dysregulation of m6A is closely associated with tumorigenesis and therapeutic resistance. As the core catalytic component of the m6A methyltransferase complex, METTL3 is aberrantly expressed in various malignancies, particularly in non-small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer, although its effects are highly context-dependent.
AIM: This review summarizes the biological functions of METTL3 in solid tumors and the preclinical and clinical development of METTL3 small-molecule inhibitors.
KEY FINDINGS: METTL3 regulates tumor progression and therapeutic resistance through m6A-dependent remodeling of oncogenic and immune transcripts. Small-molecule inhibitors, represented by STM2457 and its clinical derivative STC-15, show antitumor activity and can reverse drug resistance when combined with chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. Notably, METTL3 inhibition also mitigates chemotherapy-induced organ toxicity, suggesting a dual therapeutic benefit that may broaden the treatment window.
CONCLUSION: METTL3 is a promising but context-dependent therapeutic target; patient stratification and carefully defined therapeutic windows will be essential for clinical translation.

items.title: Genomic ascertainment of PALB2-related cancer predisposition.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer risk arising from a germline pathogenic PALB2 variant ascertained through a personal or family history of cancer has been well-studied. Here, we used genomic ascertainment to quantify PALB2-associated cancer risk, age-specific penetrance, all-cause and cancer-specific mortality.
METHODS: We conducted a case-control study in two large population-based adult cohorts: the UK Biobank (n = 469,580) and Geisinger MyCode (n = 167,050). PALB2 P/LP heterozygotes were identified via exome sequencing and compared with non-carriers. Cancer diagnoses and vital status were obtained from linked registry and electronic health record data. We used multivariable logistic regression to estimate odds ratios for cancer outcomes and Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios for all-cause mortality. Age-specific cumulative incidence (penetrance) was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Models were adjusted for birth year, sex (when applicable), smoking status, and body mass index.
RESULTS: PALB2 P/LP variant prevalence was 1:571 in UK Biobank and 1:940 in MyCode, with the higher prevalence in the UK cohort driven by the PALB2 p.Trp1038Ter founder variant. Compared with non-carriers, heterozygotes had significantly increased odds of any cancer, female breast cancer and pancreatic cancer, in both cohorts (P < 0.01). Adjusted hazard ratios for any cancer and female breast cancer ranged from 1.7 to 3.6. All-cause mortality was increased among PALB2-heterozygotes (HR 1.61-1.67), and survival after cancer diagnosis was reduced. Family history further modified cancer risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Genomic ascertainment of PALB2-heterozygotes identifies elevated risk for multiple cancers and increased all-cause and cancer-specific mortality, although risks were lower than estimates from familial ascertainment.

items.title: Single-Atom Pt-Anchored MoOx Matrix for On-Tissue Calibration in Quantitative Mass Spectrometry Imaging.
items.abstract: Quantitative mass spectrometry imaging (qMSI) enables spatially resolved metabolite profiling in biological tissues, yet reliable concentration mapping remains constrained by high matrix-derived background interference, limited metabolite coverage, and insufficient calibration robustness. To overcome these challenges, a single-atom platinum-anchored molybdenum oxide matrix (denoted as Ptsa/MoOx) was developed for qMSI. Compared with conventional organic matrices, the Ptsa/MoOx matrix not only substantially enhances metabolite ion signals but also effectively suppresses low-mass background interference. Comprehensive structural characterization revealed oxygen-deficient MoOx with highly dispersed Pt single atoms, and mechanistic investigation indicated that charge-mediated desorption and ionization contribute to the enhanced matrix performance. Using Ptsa/MoOx-assisted qMSI, an on-tissue calibration strategy was established across a wide polarity range of metabolites, achieving excellent linear responses from 43 to 853 ng mm-2. For metabolites lacking authentic standards, a class-matched concentration-referencing strategy was applied to generate concentration-referenced spatial maps for 124 metabolites. Application to five paired pancreatic tumor and adjacent non-tumor specimens demonstrated region-dependent differences across multiple lipid-related pathways as a proof-of-concept tissue application. Collectively, these results establish Ptsa/MoOx-assisted qMSI as an on-tissue calibrated platform for spatial metabolomics and demonstrate its potential for characterizing metabolic heterogeneity in biological tissues.

items.title: What Not to Miss or Misdiagnose on Abdominal and Pelvic Imaging: A Case-Based Approach and Literature Review.
items.abstract: This article, case-based review examines high-impact abdominopelvic imaging findings that are frequently missed or misinterpreted. Major themes include vascular emergencies, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, gynecologic, and traumatic pitfalls, edge-of-field lesions, and subtle manifestations of malignancy such as early pancreatic cancer, mucinous liver metastases, and incidental bladder, rectal, breast, testicular, and endometrial tumors. It emphasizes common blind spots, perceptual and interpretive errors, and cognitive biases contributing to diagnostic failure. Practical strategies are outlined, including structured search patterns, routine use of multiplanar reformations and prior comparisons, close integration of clinical data, and judicious use of advanced imaging and artificial intelligence tools to reduce error.

items.title: Malignant melanoma of unknown primary mimicking pancreatic cancer diagnosed by EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy: NRAS mutation and a rare KIT exon 17 variant.
FAM83D in cancer: Molecular mechanisms, biomarker potential and future therapeutic perspectives (Review).
items.abstract: Family with sequence similarity 83 member D (FAM83D) is a member of the FAM83 protein family characterized by a conserved domain of unknown function 1669 domain. Initially recognized for its role in mitotic spindle organization and cell-cycle regulation, FAM83D has increasingly emerged as a cancer-associated protein. FAM83D is frequently upregulated in multiple malignancies, including lung, hepatocellular, ovarian, breast, gastric, colorectal, esophageal and pancreatic cancer. Elevated FAM83D expression is associated with tumor progression, lymph node metastasis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, therapeutic resistance and worse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, FAM83D may promote malignant phenotypes by regulating cell-cycle progression, interacting with casein kinase 1 isoforms, kinesin family member 22 and F-box/WD repeat-containing protein 7, and modulating oncogenic pathways such as MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β/SMAD signaling. There may be an association between FAM83D and the tumor immune microenvironment, although direct mechanistic evidence remains limited. Clinically, FAM83D may have value as a diagnostic or prognostic biomarker and as a potential therapeutic target. However, the majority of available evidence comes from public database analyses, retrospective tissue studies and preclinical models, while large-scale prospective validation and standardized detection methods are lacking. The present review summarizes the biological features, expression patterns, functional roles, regulatory mechanisms, clinical implications, limitations and future research directions for FAM83D in cancer.

items.title: Myocardial infarction risk across cancer subtypes - a nationwide registry-based follow-up study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: As cancer survival improves, a growing population of patients is exposed to elevated cardiovascular risk. We compared the one-year risk of myocardial infarction (MI) across 13 cancer types using patients with low-risk skin tumors as a cancer-active reference group.
METHODS: In this nationwide registry-based cohort study, we included 660,531 Danish patients diagnosed with one of 13 cancer subtypes between 2000 and 2023. Patients with prior MI or coronary revascularization were excluded. Standardized one-year absolute risks of MI were estimated using the Aalen-Johansen estimator with inverse probability of treatment weighting, while relative risks were estimated using g-computation based on cause-specific Cox models for MI and all-cause death.
RESULTS: Compared with patients with low-risk skin tumors, the relative risk of MI was highest in multiple myeloma (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.34-2.26), bladder cancer (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.26-1.78), kidney cancer (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.20-1.82), leukemia (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.16-1.75), and gastrointestinal cancer (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.24-1.50). Standardized one-year MI risk remained below 1% across all cancer subtypes, ranging from 0.31% in breast cancer to 0.91% in multiple myeloma. One-year all-cause mortality varied markedly across cancer subtypes, from 2.2% in patients with low-risk skin tumors to 71.9% in patients with hepatobiliary and pancreatic cancer.
CONCLUSIONS: One-year MI risk varied across cancer subtypes. Relative and standardized absolute MI risks were highest in patients with multiple myeloma, with increased risks also observed in several other cancer subtypes. These findings represent MI risk in the presence of substantial competing mortality and should not be interpreted as differences in underlying biological susceptibility to MI.

items.title: Predictors of Fecal Elastase Testing Completion in Outpatient and Inpatient Settings: A Single Center Retrospective Analysis.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To characterize completion of fecal elastase-1 (FE-1) testing, identify clinical contexts associated with abnormal results, evaluate downstream diagnostic and treatment events, and determine the clinical significance of non-completion.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with FE-1 orders from 2017 through 2022 in a large integrated health system. Orders placed within 30 days were consolidated into diagnostic episodes. Completion required a linked specimen with a reported result. We evaluated pre-order clinical contexts and one-year outcomes and performed a weighted manual chart review of 200 unique patients with non-completed episodes sampled from four downstream pathway strata.
RESULTS: Among 23,422 diagnostic episodes, 11,834 (50.5%) were completed. FE-1 ≤200 µg/g occurred in 20.4% of interpretable results and varied by clinical context: 13.7% with irritable bowel syndrome, 21.2% with chronic diarrhea, 38.3% with chronic pancreatitis, 60.1% with pancreatic cancer, and 79.5% after pancreatic surgery. Initial completion was associated with higher odds of new exocrine pancreatic insufficiency diagnosis (adjusted odds ratio, 2.27; 95% confidence interval, 1.91-2.70) and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy initiation (adjusted odds ratio, 2.20; 95% confidence interval, 1.89-2.55), whereas non-completion was associated with more repeat FE-1 testing. Among eligible unique non-completers, weighted chart review classified 66.9% as probable missed diagnostic follow-through based on available documentation; failure to submit or return the specimen (60.1%) and specimen-processing problems (20.4%) predominated.
CONCLUSIONS: FE-1 completion was modestly associated with measured pre-order factors, while abnormal results varied substantially by clinical context. Specimen return, processing, and closed-loop follow-up represent potential targets for improving evaluation of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

items.title: SVP Maps Spatially Variable Functional Programs and Their Coupling in Spatial Transcriptomics.
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has made tissue architecture measurable at molecular resolution, yet most computational methods still identify spatially variable genes and infer biology only indirectly. We present SVP, a framework that directly maps spatially variable cell states, pathways and regulatory programs from spatial transcriptomic data. SVP combines location-level functional activity inference with global and local spatial autocorrelation and extends these analyses to bivariate spatial coupling across heterogeneous features. Across simulations and real datasets, SVP recovered cell-state-associated activity patterns at individual captured locations, detected spatially variable features with calibrated statistics, and scaled efficiently to large datasets. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, SVP identified a spatially co-organized hypoxic and extracellular-matrix-remodeling niche that co-localized with regions of low immune activity. It further captured functional maturation in the developing human heart and plaque-associated glial programs in Alzheimer's disease models. SVP enables direct analysis of functional spatial organization, moving beyond gene-centric descriptions of tissue structure.

items.title: [Research progress of irreversible electroporation for pancreatic cancer].
[Endoscopic ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors].
items.abstract: Endoscopic ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation (EUS-RFA) is an emerging minimally invasive treatment for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, particularly insulinomas. Traditionally, insulinomas are managed surgically, often requiring major pancreatic resections associated with significant morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and the risk of long-term complications including pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes. We report the initial clinical experience with EUS-RFA at a tertiary center in Sweden, including three patients with symptomatic insulinomas. All patients underwent successful EUS-RFA with short procedure times, minimal postoperative care and no major complications. Hypoglycemic symptoms resolved in all cases, and follow-up imaging showed no residual tumor activity. These findings align with emerging international data suggesting that EUS-RFA is a safe and effective alternative to surgery for selected patients with low-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The technique may reduce the need for extensive surgery and the associated healthcare burden, while improving patient quality of life. Although further prospective and randomized studies are needed to establish long-term outcomes and optimal patient selection, EUS-RFA has the potential to represent a paradigm shift in the management of insulinomas and other selected pancreatic lesions.

items.title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis.
items.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA -Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Openweight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama , Mistral , Qwen , Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.
CODE AND DATA: github.com/sarkar-lab/SPARTA_public.

items.title: Phenome-wide associations of CT-derived adipose area and density in 22,710 patients: uncovering unexpected disease connections
items.abstract: Adipose tissue plays a central role in metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis, yet its quantity and composition are rarely characterized together in routine care. We performed a phenome-wide association study linking abdominal CT scans from 22,710 patients at two tertiary care centers to electronic health record phenotypes. Subcutaneous and visceral fat area indices (SFI, VFI) and densities (SFD, VFD) were derived with a validated deep learning pipeline and tested against 624 phenotypes (2,496 tests). We identified 922 Bonferroni-significant associations across 60% (373/624) of phenotypes, recapitulating established relationships with morbid obesity (SFI odds ratio [OR] = 1.60), type 2 diabetes (VFI OR = 1.57), cirrhosis (VFD OR = 3.56) and pancreatic cancer (SFI OR = 0.56). Across the phenome, area and density odds ratios were inversely correlated (r = − 0.80), as expected for markers inversely correlated within each depot. When modelled jointly, density remained associated with disease independently of area for 90% (351/392) of phenotypes with a joint adipose association, whereas area was informative beyond density for 35% (136/392) and without density for 2% (6/392). These findings provide a hypothesis-generating atlas in which adipose density emerges as a candidate biomarker of systemic physiology. All analysis code and results are openly available (https://atesfet.github.io/fatwas.io).

items.title: Beyond organ-based therapy: Genome-directed treatment of metastatic gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (GEA) is a rare, HPV-independent subtype of cervical cancer associated with aggressive behavior and poor response to conventional treatment for cervical cancer. Optimal management is hindered by limited clinical trial data specific to this rare cancer subtype. Genomic analysis holds the promise of identifying better therapy and improving outcomes in this and other rare diseases.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 81-year-old woman presented with vaginal discharge and postmenopausal bleeding and was diagnosed with HPV-independent GEA. Imaging demonstrated a locally advanced cervical mass and a concurrent pancreatic tail lesion, raising concern for either metastatic cervical cancer or a synchronous primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Comparative next-generation sequencing demonstrated identical pathogenic alterations in KRAS and TP53, strongly supporting a shared clonal origin. Integration of the clinical, pathologic, and molecular findings favored metastatic GEA with a pancreatic-like phenotype, and pancreatic cancer-directed chemotherapy was initiated. The patient received gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel and achieved a complete radiographic and metabolic response after six cycles. She subsequently underwent laparoscopic hysterectomy, with only microscopic residual disease at the cervicovaginal margin.
CONCLUSIONS: Comparative molecular profiling may help clarify the relationship between tumors at different anatomic sites and inform individualized treatment selection in diagnostically challenging cases of GEA. The observed response to pancreatic cancer-directed chemotherapy in this case is hypothesis-generating and requires further investigation.

items.title: Acquired Hemophilia A Diagnosed after Repeated Postoperative Bleeding Following Pancreatectomy: A Report of Two Cases.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Acquired hemophilia A (AHA) is a rare autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by the development of autoantibodies against factor VIII, resulting in decreased factor VIII activity, and isolated prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). AHA is often diagnosed after the onset of bleeding and may follow a fatal course due to uncontrolled hemorrhage or infectious complications associated with immunosuppressive therapy. Although early diagnosis is essential, the rarity of the disease makes it difficult. We report 2 cases of AHA diagnosed after repeated postoperative bleeding following pancreatectomy.
CASE PRESENTATION: Case 1. An 80-year-old man underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy for ampullary cancer. Postoperatively, he developed recurrent bleeding from the surgical site, requiring repeated interventional radiology procedures until POD 12. Persistent prolongation of APTT that did not correct with transfusion suggested a coagulation disorder. On POD 13, laboratory testing demonstrated decreased factor VIII activity and the presence of a factor VIII inhibitor, confirming the diagnosis of AHA. Despite treatment with recombinant activated factor VII for bleeding, he passed away on POD 34 due to repeated bleeding, infected ascites, and subsequent sepsis. Case 2. An 83-year-old man underwent distal pancreatectomy with celiac axis resection for locally advanced pancreatic cancer. Postoperative anemia progressed with persistent prolongation of APTT despite repeated transfusions. Based on the experience from Case 1, AHA was suspected early. On POD 8, decreased factor VIII activity and the presence of a factor VIII inhibitor confirmed the diagnosis of AHA, and immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone was initiated immediately. The factor VIII inhibitor became undetectable on POD 36, and the patient was discharged on POD 123.
CONCLUSIONS: Delayed diagnosis of AHA after invasive surgery such as pancreatectomy may be fatal. AHA should be considered in cases of repeated postoperative bleeding with the prolongation of APTT.

items.title: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with atypical biliary obstruction secondary to tension pneumobilia: a case report.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Most patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer present with constitutional syndrome, abdominal pain, and/or jaundice. Jaundice is typically due to tumor-induced biliary obstruction. However, as we will illustrate in our clinical case, rare obstructive mechanisms can sometimes occur.
CASE PRESENTATION: We present the case of a 63-year-old woman diagnosed with borderline resectable ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head. The clinical presentation included obstructive jaundice and altered liver function tests. During the neoadjuvant therapy preparation and despite prior adequate biliary stenting via endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), the patient experienced a new episode of progressive hyperbilirubinemia in the absence of obstructive biliary dilatation or stent dysfunction. Following investigations, this was attributed to functional obstruction secondary to trapped tension pneumobilia visible on cross-sectional imaging. Following multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient underwent a percutaneous cholecystostomy with drainage of the trapped air. This procedure successfully achieved subsequent bilirubin normalization, and the patient was able to continue successfully neoadjuvant mFOLFIRINOX chemotherapy, followed by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) with curative intent. She remains cancer-free.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights the importance of considering differential diagnoses in biliary obstruction in patients with patent biliary stents, as well as the relevance of a multidisciplinary approach in borderline resectable pancreatic tumors.

items.title: [Gastroenterology in Israel: quality, innovation, and prevention].
items.abstract: This issue of Harefuah highlights the breadth of contemporary gastroenterology in Israel, spanning the Mediterranean diet in irritable bowel syndrome, gastrointestinal complications of diabetes, future therapies for celiac disease, and the central role of colonoscopy quality metrics and adequate bowel preparation. Alongside these reviews and position statements, the issue includes case reports that emphasize a broad differential diagnosis and complex therapeutic solutions, including Wernicke encephalopathy as a presenting feature of celiac disease, primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, and severe malnutrition after gastric bypass surgery. It also presents a position paper on surveillance of individuals at increased risk for pancreatic malignancy, defining risk groups, recommended workup and multidisciplinary follow-up, while underscoring the importance of reducing modifiable risk factors.

Expansion of the MEN1 tumor spectrum: convergent molecular evidence of MEN1 inactivation in a fibromyxosarcoma, VIPoma, and gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominant tumor predisposition syndrome primarily characterized by parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreaticoduodenal neuroendocrine tumors. Although several non-endocrine neoplasms have been associated with MEN1, the role of MEN1 inactivation in rare mesenchymal tumors remains incompletely understood.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a woman with genetically confirmed MEN1 carrying the pathogenic germline MEN1 variant c.249_252delGTCT (p.Ile85Serfs*33, exon 2), identified in a large MEN1 kindred. The patient presented with primary hyperparathyroidism, a non-functioning pituitary microadenoma, a pancreatic vasoactive intestinal peptide-producing neuroendocrine tumor (VIPoma), and a poorly differentiated gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma. The VIPoma was successfully cured by gastroduodenopancreatectomy, with complete resolution of the WDHA syndrome and normalization of serum VIP levels. In contrast, the gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma followed an aggressive clinical course, leading to disease recurrence and death 30 months after surgery. In addition, the patient developed a recurrent low-grade odontogenic fibromyxosarcoma of the maxilla. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated complete loss of nuclear menin expression in the fibromyxosarcoma, pancreatic VIPoma, and gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma. Molecular analyses of the fibromyxosarcoma revealed allelic imbalance at the MEN1 locus by Sanger sequencing, with apparent absence of the wild-type allele at exon 2 and exclusive detection of the T allele of an informative heterozygous synonymous MEN1 variant (c.1269C>T; p.Asp418=, exon 9). Targeted next-generation sequencing confirmed marked enrichment of the mutant MEN1 allele in the fibromyxosarcoma (VAF 81.8%) and demonstrated enrichment of the mutant allele in the VIPoma (VAF 68.2%) and gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma (VAF 70.6%). Together with loss of menin expression by immunohistochemistry, these findings support somatic MEN1 inactivation across all three tumors.
CONCLUSIONS: This report provides convergent genetic and immunohistochemical evidence supporting low-grade odontogenic fibromyxosarcoma as a potential MEN1-associated neoplasm. In addition, the demonstration of MEN1 inactivation across three exceptionally rare tumors arising in the same patient provides evidence for a broader role of menin loss across distinct tumor types and supports the possibility that the phenotypic spectrum of MEN1 extends beyond currently recognized manifestations.
